newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh expects economic growth above 5.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh expects economic growth above 5.5 pct.

text.p: Bangladesh Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria said on Tuesday that the country's economy was on right track and might grow more than 5.5 percent in fiscal 1996/97 ending in June.
"We expect slightly higher than targetted 5.5 percent economic growth this year," he told members of the Overseas Correspondents Association of Bangladesh.
Kibria said his government was working on reforms in privatisation, banking and legal sectors to boost the economy, which he said was growing steadily but not as fast as expected.
"I do not want to paint a rosy picture about the economy. But what I can say is that it is growing steadily," he said.
"We must improve the efficiency of the government to raise the economic growth."
Bangladesh's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 4.7 percent in 1995/96.
Kibria said inflation was under control, both exports and imports were rising, and the country has generally sound foreign exchange reserves.
He said better economic management and higher food production helped wrestle the inflation rate to 2.71 percent at end-Decemeber from 5.81 percent in 1995.
"Inflation destroys not only the economy but also the social fabrics. The rate of inflation has now deminished because of our prudent financial management," he said.
Kibria said: "The country's banks are groaning under bad loans. We are closing legal loopholes to crack down on bank defaulters."
Government officials said private and public companies had defaulted on about $3.5 billion in bank loans.
The minister said foreign exchange reserves were steady at $1.98 billion, equal to three and half months of the country's imports.
But reserves were down from $3.07 billion in June 1995 and $2.04 billion in June 1996.
"There has been unusual credit growth in the past several months that led to a colossal loss of reserves," Kibria said.

Credit to public and private sectors grew to 15.3 billion taka ($360 million) in the first five months of the current fisacl year to November against only 8.6 billion taka ($204 million) in the same period of 1995/96, official figures show.

But the finance minister said there had been a better growth in remittance from Bangladeshis working abroad. In July-December remittances totalled $781.77 million compared with $556.84 million in same period of 1995/96.
"I hope the workers' remittance is playing an import role in our reserves position," he said.
He said foreign aid disbursement was satisfactory this year. The annual foreign aid flow remains around $1.7 billion a year.
The finance minister also said there had been a good response from investors with some 46 countries registering $3.85 billion in investment this year.
